content.title: Do I have new Cicada COVID, flu, RSV, or cold? Symptoms, differences
content.text: March 31, 2026, 2:39 p.m. ETThe CDC reports a highly mutated Cicada COVID variant BA 3.2 has been detected in at least 25 states including New Jersey in what could result in a summer surge of new COVID-19 cases, colliding with flu, cold and allergy season as respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains high.But what are the symptoms of the Cicada COVID variant, and how do current COVID-19 symptoms 2026 compare? Not sure if you have the common cold, flu, COVID or RSV symptoms? As the CDC reports cases of the new virus COVID-19 variant Cicada — so called for remaining "underground" for years — in NJ, Pennsylvania, New York, Maryland and across the Northeast, here's the latest on what virus is going around right now and see the difference between cold vs. flu vs. COVID symptoms.Influenza B (flu B), RSV and COVID-19 activity is elevated with outbreaks in long-term care facilities, with outbreaks of the flu reported in New Jersey schools, according to the latest NJ Health Department data on respiratory illnesses, ending March 21.Do I have flu B symptoms? How long do COVID symptoms last? Here's what you need to know about the symptoms for COVID-19, RSV, flu and the common cold.Symptoms of 'Cicada' COVID variant; COVID-19 symptomsThe new COVID variant BA 3.2 Cicada symptoms are similar to other COVID variants circulating right now like Omicron and include cough, fever or chills, sore throat, congestion, shortness of breath, loss of smell or taste, fatigue, headache, and gastrointestinal symptoms, per the CDC.The new COVID-19 variant looks different to your immune system due to so many genetic mutations, which could reduce your protection to the COVID vaccine, according to the CDC's latest Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.Flu symptoms 2026; Flu A vs flu B symptomsThe most common and most severe flu strains are influenza A and influenza B, according to the CDC, although both differ in their symptoms. Flu test positivity remains elevated in NJ, with flu B the predominant circulating virus, the NJ DOH said.Is there a difference between flu A vs flu B symptoms? Flu A is known to cause more severe illness and have been known to cause pandemics, such as the 1918 flu pandemic that led to 50 million deaths worldwide. Flu B, or type B, however, can be just as serious for babies, older adults and those immunocompromised.Flu symptoms in adults and children come on quick and symptoms last a few days to two weeks, with fatigue and chills to start, followed by fever, body aches, cough, headache, sore throat, congestion, and (runny or stuffy nose), according to the Cleveland Clinic. A fever is considered 100.4 degrees or higher, says Harvard Medical School, and a high fever is 102.4 degrees or higher.Cold vs flu vs COVIDCOVID-19, spring allergies, the common cold, and the flu can cause many of the same symptoms. Do I have COVID-19 symptoms, or are these symptoms of the new COVID-19 variant, or is it flu B?The Mayo Clinic provides a chart with the symptom differences between COVID-19, cold, allergies, and the flu here. In short, symptoms can be mild or severe, and overlapping symptoms is likely, so it's best to get testing done.When it comes to COVID vs flu, some people experience a loss of taste and smell. But COVID-19 comes on gradually, while flu hits hard and fast. Muscles aches are fever are sometimes or commonly reported in COVID-19 and flu, but not always in a cold. But a cough is common for all three, and sometimes with allergies. Head to this chart for another breakdown of COVID vs flu vs cold.RSV symptomsRespiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes cold-like symptoms, or in some cases, severe illness in babies, children and older adults, per the Cleveland Clinic. RSV symptoms include cough, trouble breathing, pauses in breathing in young infants, runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, sore throat, headache, fatigue, fever, and loss of appetite.Babies or young kids may seem fussy or irritable and might not want to play when they usually would. Head to an urgent care if you or your child has wheezing or noisy breathing, or has shortness of breath, bluish or grayish skin, lips or nails, and skin pulling in between ribs (a sign of retractions).Lori Comstock is a New Jersey-based news reporter covering trending news with USA TODAY Network's Mid-Atlantic Connect Team. She covers health and other news in the Northeast, including New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Washington DC, Maryland, and Virginia. Reach her at LComstock@usatodayco.com.
